extracted.intended_audience: journalists, photo editors, museum visitors and the general public interested in documentary/photojournalism ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the authenticity and ethical integrity of news photographs, including digital manipulation, caption accuracy, provenance, editorial response, and public accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: No digital manipulation of news photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers must not alter the substantive content of news images (e.g., by cloning or darkening elements) to misrepresent events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from the page: 'Adnan Hajj ... used Photoshop to clone and darken the smoke to exaggerate bombing damage by Israeli warplanes.' Anti-pattern: manipulating smoke/building damage to exaggerate an event. Such content-altering edits are grounds for withdrawal of images and disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate captioning / representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions and representations accompanying photographs must accurately reflect what the image shows and not imply altered or exaggerated conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page contrast: Representation — Original Reuters caption: 'Smoke billows from burning buildings destroyed during an overnight Israeli air raid...' vs REALITY — the photographer manipulated the image. Captions should match verified reality; mismatch is deceptive and undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve originals and provenance for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations and photographers should retain original, unmanipulated files so images can be compared and provenance verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page displays both the 'Manipulated photo' and 'Un-manipulated photo' and a 'Notice sent to editors after the discovery,' illustrating the need to keep originals as evidence for investigations and corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose permissible minor edits and avoid content changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor corrective edits (e.g., dust removal, lighting fixes) may be permissible but must not change the content of the scene; such edits should be disclosed when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The photographer's claim: 'he was merely trying to remove a speck of dust and fix the lighting.' Guidance implied by the incident: permitted basic retouching is distinct from content alteration (cloning/darkening smoke) and must be limited and transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue corrections, notices and public accountability when manipulation is found
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulation is discovered, news organizations must notify editors and the public and issue corrections or retractions as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page notes a 'Notice sent to editors after the discovery' and references Reuters' response; corrective steps include withdrawing images, public statements, and formal notices to editors and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial accountability and disciplinary action
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should take disciplinary action against staff who breach image ethics, up to termination, and should withdraw manipulated content from distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Reuters immediately fired Mr. Hajj and withdrew all 920 photographs by the photographer from its database after it was discovered that he had manipulated a second photo.' This demonstrates enforcement measures for violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen and enforce agency policies after incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations should revise and tighten editorial policies and procedures in response to manipulation scandals to prevent recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced item: 'Reuters toughens rules after altered photo affair' — implying that policy revision and tighter enforcement are an appropriate institutional response after such breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of external scrutiny and watchdogs in verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent public scrutiny (e.g., blogs, watchdogs) can play a role in detecting manipulations and prompting inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page documents discovery by Little Green Footballs and cites The New York Times: 'Bloggers Drive Inquiry on How Altered Images Saw Print.' Guidance: encourage responsiveness to credible external challenges and incorporate external reporting into verification workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper crediting and copyright attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs must carry correct photographer credit and copyright information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page displays 'PHOTO BY ADNAN HAJJ' and 'Image copyright Adan Hajj.' Proper crediting is standard practice and remains required even when an image is under investigation or retracted.
